title-group.article-title: Fritillaria mardinensis (Liliaceae), a New Species from Southeastern Türkiye †

abstract.p: Fritillaria mardinensis Balos, C. Çeçen, Köse & Sonay sp. nov. (Liliaceae) is described as a new species from Mardin Province, southeastern Türkiye. It is morphologically similar to F. armena and F. zagrica but differs from the related species F. armena and F. zagrica by its longer stem structure, yellowish hairy/striped mosaic pattern at the tepal tips, linear nectary structure, and capsule morphology containing longitudinally dark green striped, winged seeds. Diagnostic characters, description, detailed illustration, geographical distribution, conservation assessment, observations and taxonomic comments regarding the new species are given. ITS sequence data are compatible with the placement of the species in Fritillaria but are uninformative at the species level, as F. mardinensis falls in an unresolved polytomy with F. armena and other congeners; its delimitation therefore rests on morphology.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Fritillaria L. is the second largest genus in the Liliaceae family, with 179 species found in the North Temperate Zone [1,2,3].

Türkiye is recognized as the country with the highest diversity of Fritillaria species and endemic taxa worldwide [4]. Regarding the geographical distribution and species diversity of this genus, three main centers stand out: California (21 species), China (24 species), and the Southwest Asia–Eastern Mediterranean region (117 species). The last of these is particularly notable; Türkiye hosts 63 species, followed by Iran with 27 species and Greece with 26 species [2,3,4,5,6,7]. With this study, the number of species in Türkiye rises to 64, including 40 endemics.

The Eastern and Southeastern Anatolia Region of Türkiye, where Fritillaria mardinensis was discovered, is one of the less researched regions in terms of plant taxonomy and diversity. Many new Fritillaria species [2,3,8,9] have recently been described from this region.

During field trips conducted in March 2024 in the Zınnar and Bakırkıre localities of Mardin, the authors—with the exception of the third author—encountered an interesting Fritillaria species. Although it resembled Fritillaria armena Boiss. in terms of morphological characteristics, it differed in several characters, notably its taller stem, broadly obovate-spathulate outer tepals, inner tepals with a distinctive pigmentation pattern, yellow apical stripes and ciliate tufts on the tepals, and linear nectaries. Following consultation with the third author, a detailed morphological comparison and an ITS-based molecular study were carried out, and the species was concluded to be new on the basis of its morphology.

sec.title: 2.1. Plant Material and Morphological Examination
sec.p: About 30 specimens were collected in this study from the type locality (Bakırkıre), and all measurements were taken from this material; plants were also observed at Zınnar, but no specimens were collected there. Species identification was based on a comparative analysis of standard Fritillaria taxonomic literature and diagnostic characters. Flora of Türkiye and the East Aegean Islands [10] and Illustrated Flora of Türkiye [7] were used for the identification of the collected samples. The following taxonomic literature was also consulted: Boissier [11], Post and Dinsmore [12], Losina-Losinskaja [5], Rix [6,10], Wendelbo [13], Rechinger [14], Chen and Mordak [15], Tekşen and Aytaç [16], Tekşen [7], Advay and Tekşen [17], Eker and Tekşen [18], Sonay et al. [8,9,19], Eker and Balos [20], Advay [21], Advay et al. [22], Advay and Rix [23], Balos et al. [24], Tekşen et al. [25], Duman and Tekşen [26], Tel [27], Sonay [28], Yapar and Tekşen [29] and Balos et al. [2]. The habitat and general view of F. mardinensis are shown in Figure 1. Qualitative and quantitative morphological characters used for identification in this new Fritillaria species were analyzed with a stereo-binocular microscope (TT Technic, Türkiye) on fresh material (Figure 2). For each specimen, the presence of yellow tessellation, the tricolorous, mosaic-like pattern, and the yellow apical stripes and ciliate tufts on the tepals was recorded. Obtained findings were compared with those of the related species (Section 3.1). The names of the species were checked using the IPNI database [30]. Threat category assessment of the new species was made according to IUCN criteria [31]. Specimens were pressed, dried using standard herbarium techniques, and deposited in the HUEH (Harran University Faculty of Pharmacy Herbarium) and ESSE (Anadolu University, Faculty of Pharmacy Herbarium). Life Science Identifier (LSID) is: urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77413095-1.

sec.title: 2.2. DNA Extraction, Amplification and Sequencing
sec.p: Total genomic DNA was isolated from silica gel-preserved leaves of Fritillaria mardinensis and F. armena using the EurX GeneMATRIX Plant & Fungi DNA isolation kit (Gdańsk, Poland; https://eurx.com.pl, accessed on 4 November 2026) following the manufacturer’s instructions. To amplify the nuclear ribosomal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region, encompassing ITS1, 5.8S and ITS2, we utilized the universal primers ITS1 and ITS4 [32]. The amplification was carried out in a thermal cycler (Thermo Scientific, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) under the PCR parameters established by Balos et al. [2]. Following verification of the PCR products via 1% agarose gel electrophoresis, bidirectional sequencing was conducted by BM Labosis (Ankara, Türkiye; https://www.bmlabosis.com/en/, accessed on 4 November 2026). Forward (ITS1) and reverse (ITS4) reads were assembled for each sample. The ITS sequences used in the analyses are provided in Supplementary File S1. The sequence of F. mardinensis analyzed here was 458 bp long. For F. armena, the forward read was of low quality over part of its length, and positions with low-quality or ambiguous peaks were coded as N, yielding a partial consensus sequence of 588 positions (472 unambiguous sites). The two ITS sequences newly generated in this study (F. mardinensis and F. armena) (Table 1) were submitted to GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/, accessed on 4 November 2026) and received the submission IDs D49CD61U016 and D49HRX46014, respectively; GenBank accession numbers will be provided once assigned, and the records will be publicly released upon publication of this article. For comparative purposes, additional ITS sequences of allied Fritillaria species were retrieved from GenBank (Appendix A, Table A1). Two GenBank records are available for F. zagrica (KM435235 and KM435236) [33], both derived from clones. These sequences contained rearranged segments that are inconsistent with the arrangement of ITS in other Fritillaria species; only the collinear region of KM435235 (positions 262–640; 379 bp) was therefore included in the analysis.

sec.title: 2.3. Sequence Alignment and Phylogenetic Analysis
sec.p: Multiple sequence alignment of the ITS dataset (18 taxa) was performed using ClustalW [34] implemented in MEGA 12.0 [35] and manually adjusted. Because the sequence of F. mardinensis (458 bp), the partial consensus of F. armena and the region of F. zagrica used (379 bp) were shorter than most other sequences (ca. 600–800 bp), sites with missing data were treated with partial deletion (site coverage cut-off 50%) in the ML analysis.

Maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic analysis was conducted using MEGA [35]. The best-fitting nucleotide substitution model was selected based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) calculated in MEGA. Among the 24 models tested, K2+I [36] was selected as the best-fitting model (BIC = 4240; lnL = −1958). The ML tree was inferred with 1000 bootstrap pseudo-replicates to evaluate nodal robustness [37]. Lilium martagon AF088203.1 was designated as the outgroup. Nodes with bootstrap support below 50% were collapsed in the final tree.

sec.title: 3.1. Taxonomic Treatment
sec.p: Fritillaria mardinensis Balos, C. Çeçen, Köse & Sonay sp. nov. (Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3, Table 2).
Type: Türkiye. Mardin: Northeast of Old Mardin, Bakırkıre locality, stony north-facing slopes, 28 March 2024, M. Balos 5562 (holotype HUEH, isotypes ESSE).

Diagnosis: Fritillaria mardinensis is most similar to F. armena and F. zagrica. It differs from F. armena by its taller stem (11.5–23.0 cm vs. 4.0–15.0 cm long), broadly obovate-spathulate, obtuse outer tepals (vs. lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate or oblong, acute), inner tepals with a blackish-purple median stripe and deep vinaceous-red margins (forming a mosaic-like pattern in about 10 of the ca. 30 specimens examined, mainly at early anthesis), and tepals consistently tessellated with yellow, with yellow apical stripes and short yellowish ciliate tufts (vs. tepals dark purple on both surfaces and pruinose outside), and linear nectaries 4.0–7.0 × 0.5–1.0 mm (vs. lanceolate, 3.0–6.0 × 1.0–1.5 mm). It differs from F. zagrica by its taller stem (11.5–23.0 cm vs. 4.0–12.0 cm long), lower leaves without undulate margins (vs. undulate), broadly obovate-spathulate, obtuse outer tepals (vs. ovate-lanceolate, acute), narrowly oblanceolate, acute inner tepals (vs. oblanceolate, obtuse), longer linear nectaries 4.0–7.0 mm long (vs. lanceolate, ca. 3.0 mm long), and purple, narrowly oblong to linear-oblong anthers 5.5–8.0 mm long (vs. greenish-yellow, oblong, 3.0–4.0 mm long).

Description: Perennial, bulbous plant. Bulb 1.3–1.5 × 1.3–1.5 cm, globose, with a few bulblets; tunica papery. Stem 11.5–23.0 cm long, erect, smooth. Leaves 4 (-5), sessile, green to slightly glaucous, alternate; lowest leaf 2; 4.1–11.0 × 0.4–1.5 cm, lanceolate, acute; median leaves 1; 3.0–7.8 × 0.3–0.5 cm, lanceolate, acute to acuminate. Bract 1(-2), 2.0–5.5 × 0.2–0.4 cm, linear-lanceolate, acuminate. Flowers 1(-2), nodding, perigon narrowly campanulate, 15–22 mm long, purplish; apex of the tepals with yellow stripes; tepals tessellated with yellow; outer and inner tepals ciliate-tufted with yellowish short hairs at the tips (yellow apical stripes, yellow tessellation and ciliate tufts present in all specimens examined); tepals dimorphic; outer tepals 14.5–22 × 5.5–8.25 mm, broadly obovate-spathulate, obtuse, uniformly dark purplish-black; inner tepals 14.5–22.5 × 5.1–8.0 mm, narrowly oblanceolate, acute, blackish-purple along the median stripe and deep vinaceous-red towards the margins; in about 10 of the ca. 30 specimens examined, inner tepals tricolorous, with yellowish-cream lateral zones and rose-red margins forming a mosaic-like pattern; this pattern is distinct at early anthesis and fades as the tepals darken towards the end of flowering. Nectaries 4.0–7.0 × 0.5–1.0 mm, linear, green, placed 1.0–1.5 mm above the base at the tepals. Filaments 7.0–9.5 × 1.0–1.5 mm, pale green below, pinkish above, densely papillose in the upper half; anthers 5.5–8.0 × 0.9–2.0 mm long, narrowly oblong to linear-oblong, apiculate, purple, basifixed near the bottom. Style 7.4–8.0 × 1.4–1.9 mm, yellow, not exserted from perigon; ovary 6.5–8.5 × 1.9–2.0 mm, pale green; stigma tripartite, segments 1–2.5 mm long, papillose. Capsule 3–4.3 × 1.2–1.5 cm, ovoid to obovoid, 3-locular, basally attenuate, apically rounded, longitudinally dark green-striped, green, not winged. Seeds broadly obovate to subtriangular, flattened, broadly winged, testa brown, 5.75–6.0 × 4.25–5 mm; margin light brown, center brown (Table 2).
Etymology: The specific epithet of the new species is derived from Mardin, the province where the species was found.
Vernacular name: No local name was recorded; the Turkish name for F. mardinensis is proposed as ‘zınnarlalesi’ according to the guidelines of Menemen et al. [38].

Distribution and habitat: Fritillaria mardinensis is a local endemic species restricted to Mardin province, southeastern Anatolia. It is an element of Irano–Turanian phytogeographical region. It grows on stony north-facing slopes at 1145 m a.s.l. (Figure 4). Plants were also observed, but not collected, at Zınnar. Species growing nearby are Colchicum kotschyi Boiss., Corydalis oppositifolia DC., Cerasus microcarpa subsp. tortuosa (Boiss. & Hausskn.) Browicz, Geranium dissectum L., Hyacinthella siirtensis B.Mathew, Lamium garganicum L., Muscari discolor Boiss. & Hausskn., and Sanguisorba minor Scop.
Phenology: Flowering from March and fruiting from May.

Conservation status: Less than 100 mature individuals were observed at the type locality of Fritillaria mardinensis, which covers an area of occupancy (AOO) of less than 10 km2 (criteria B2). Plants were also observed at Zınnar, 2–4 km from the type locality, but were not counted; both sites lie within this AOO (no more than two 2 × 2 km grid cells). There is a serious grazing effect on the population, which may lead to a reduction in the number of individuals in the near future. Because both sites are subject to the same grazing pressure, they are treated as a single location sensu IUCN [31]. Therefore, due to its restricted population, a single location, and estimated decrease in the area of occupancy, habitat quality and number of mature individuals, the species may be classified as “Critically Endangered” (CR) (criteria B2ab [i, ii, v]) [31].

Taxonomic relationships: Fritillaria mardinensis is morphologically allied to F. armena Boiss. and F. zagrica Stapf, but it can be distinguished from both species by a combination of vegetative, floral, and fruit characters. Although these taxa share a broadly similar habit and dark purple flowers, comparative examination reveals several diagnostic differences supporting the recognition of F. mardinensis as a distinct species.

Compared with F. armena, F. mardinensis is characterized by its generally taller stem (11.5–23.0 cm vs. 4.0–15.0 cm) and broadly obovate-spathulate outer tepals with obtuse apices, rather than lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate or oblong, and acute outer tepals. The inner tepals of F. mardinensis are narrowly oblanceolate and exhibit a distinctive pigmentation pattern, including a blackish-purple median stripe and deep vinaceous-red margins; in about 10 of the ca. 30 specimens examined, yellowish-cream lateral zones and rose-red margins produce a mosaic-like appearance, which is most distinct at early anthesis. Yellow stripes and short yellowish ciliate tufts at the tepal apices, present in all specimens examined, provide additional diagnostic characters. In contrast, the tepals of F. armena are dark purple on both surfaces and exhibit a pruinose or waxy outer surface. The nectaries of F. mardinensis are linear and relatively narrow (4.0–7.0 × 0.5–1.0 mm), whereas those of F. armena are lanceolate and broader (3.0–6.0 × 1.0–1.5 mm). Furthermore, F. mardinensis has a larger capsule (3.0–4.3 cm long) than the reported range for F. armena (1.4–3.4 cm), although these measurements overlap. The capsule of F. mardinensis is ovoid to obovoid and longitudinally striped with dark green, while its seeds are broadly winged and measure 5.75–6.0 × 4.25–5.0 mm.

The distinction between F. mardinensis and F. zagrica is supported by differences in stem length, leaf morphology, tepal shape, nectary structure, and anther morphology. Fritillaria mardinensis has a longer stem (11.5–23.0 cm) than F. zagrica (4.0–12.0 cm), and its lanceolate leaves lack the undulate margins reported for the lower leaves of F. zagrica. The outer tepals of F. mardinensis are broadly obovate-spathulate and obtuse, while those of F. zagrica are ovate-lanceolate and acute. The inner tepals of F. mardinensis are narrowly oblanceolate and acute, contrasting with the oblanceolate, obtuse inner tepals of F. zagrica. The linear, green nectaries of F. mardinensis (4.0–7.0 mm long) also differ from the shorter, lanceolate nectaries of F. zagrica (approximately 3.0 mm long). In addition, the anthers of F. mardinensis are purple and narrowly oblong to linear-oblong, whereas those of F. zagrica are greenish-yellow and oblong. The tepal pigmentation of F. mardinensis, particularly the yellow apical stripes, yellowish ciliate tufts, and occasional mosaic-like pattern, further distinguishes it from the dark purple, waxy-pruinose tepals of F. zagrica, which have yellow apices.

Taken together, these comparisons indicate that F. mardinensis is most readily recognized by the combination of a relatively elongated stem, distinctive tepal pigmentation and apical ciliation, narrow linear nectaries, purple anthers, and a longitudinally dark-striped capsule. Although individual quantitative characters overlap with those of the related species, the combined character set provides a useful morphological basis for distinguishing F. mardinensis from F. armena and F. zagrica.

sec.title: 3.2. Molecular Phylogenetic Analysis
sec.p: The ML tree based on the ITS dataset (18 taxa; 826 aligned positions; Figure 5) was rooted with Lilium martagon. All sampled Fritillaria species except F. ferganensis and F. zagrica formed a well-supported clade (bootstrap support, BS = 95); F. ferganensis and F. zagrica formed a separate pair (BS = 95), whose relationship to this clade and to the outgroup remained unresolved. Within the main clade, one lineage comprised F. usuriensis and a F. tubiformis–F. lusitanica pair (BS = 75 and 95, respectively), and the other (BS = 84) comprised F. meleagroides and a larger group (BS = 94). In the latter, F. caucasica and F. latifolia formed a strongly supported pair (BS = 100), whereas F. mardinensis, F. armena, F. alburyana, F. hermontis, F. aurea, F. reuteri, F. minuta, F. olivieri and F. crassifolia remained in an unresolved polytomy because nodes with bootstrap support below 50% were collapsed.

Fritillaria mardinensis was therefore placed within the main Fritillaria clade, but its relationships to the other species of this group, including F. armena, could not be resolved with the ITS data. Compared with the two morphologically most similar species, F. mardinensis differed by 6 bp from F. armena (over 334 compared sites; Kimura 2-parameter distance 0.02) and by 23 bp from F. zagrica (over 330 compared sites; distance 0.074). The Kimura 2-parameter distances between F. mardinensis and the other species of the polytomy ranged from 0.011 (F. alburyana) to 0.029 (F. crassifolia). The ITS distance between F. mardinensis and F. armena thus falls within the range observed between F. mardinensis and the other species of the polytomy and is larger than that to F. alburyana; ITS therefore provides no evidence for or against the separation of F. mardinensis from F. armena. For F. zagrica, only a collinear region of the available GenBank record (379 bp) was used (see Section 2.2), and F. armena was represented by a partial consensus sequence (472 unambiguous sites).

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: The new species was discovered in the Zınnar and Bakırkıre localities of Mardin Province during fieldwork conducted in March 2024. Specimens were collected and measured only at Bakırkıre (the type locality); plants at Zınnar were observed but not collected, so the morphological variation reported here refers to the Bakırkıre population. Its initial resemblance to F. armena prompted a more detailed comparative assessment, which revealed a combination of characters separating it from both F. armena and F. zagrica.

The comparative results demonstrate that the identification of F. mardinensis should not rely on a single morphological character. Stem length, for example, distinguishes it from the typical ranges reported for the related taxa only partially, because the measurements overlap. Similarly, leaf number, style length, and some tepal dimensions are not independently decisive. Instead, the taxonomic value of the new species lies in the combination of vegetative and reproductive characters, particularly tepal shape and pigmentation, nectary morphology, anther color, and capsule characteristics.

The perianth provides some of the most conspicuous diagnostic features. The broadly obovate-spathulate outer tepals and narrowly oblanceolate inner tepals of F. mardinensis differ in shape and apex morphology from the corresponding tepals of F. armena and F. zagrica. Particularly noteworthy is the variable pigmentation of the inner tepals, which may include a blackish-purple median stripe, vinaceous-red margins, yellowish-cream lateral zones, and rose-red marginal areas. This pigmentation can produce a mosaic-like pattern, while yellow apical stripes and short yellowish ciliate tufts provide additional distinguishing features. Among the ca. 30 specimens examined, yellow tessellation, the yellow apical stripes and the ciliate tufts were present in all individuals, whereas the mosaic-like pattern was observed in about 10 individuals. This pattern is distinct at early anthesis, but the tepals darken and the pattern fades towards the end of flowering; the constant characters are therefore given more weight in the diagnosis. Such characters, when assessed together with tepal shape and dimensions, are useful for the morphological delimitation of closely related species.

The nectaries and reproductive organs provide further evidence for morphological differentiation. The linear nectaries of F. mardinensis contrast with the lanceolate nectaries of the two related species, particularly in their narrower form and greater reported length relative to those of F. zagrica. Differences in anther color and shape also contribute to the comparative diagnosis. In F. mardinensis, the anthers are purple and narrowly oblong to linear-oblong, whereas those of F. zagrica are greenish-yellow and oblong. The pale green to pinkish filaments of F. mardinensis also differ from the usually yellow filaments reported for F. armena. These reproductive characters complement the external perianth features and strengthen the overall morphological diagnosis.

Fruit and seed morphology provide additional characters for identification. The capsule of F. mardinensis is relatively large, ovoid to obovoid, green, and marked by longitudinal dark green stripes. Its flattened seeds are broadly winged and broadly obovate to subtriangular. Although capsule size overlaps with the reported range of F. armena, the combination of capsule shape, longitudinal striping, and seed morphology contributes to the recognition of the new species. Further comparative examination of mature fruits and seeds from multiple populations would help establish the consistency and taxonomic significance of these characters.

The ITS-based phylogeny places F. mardinensis within the main Fritillaria clade (BS = 95), in agreement with its morphological assignment to the genus, but the ITS data are uninformative at the species level and therefore neither support nor contradict the species boundaries inferred from morphology. ITS divergence among the closely related species of this clade was low, and most internal nodes received bootstrap support below 50% and were collapsed (Figure 5). Weak bootstrap support for several clades of Eurasian Fritillaria in ITS analyses has been reported previously [39], and ITS variation alone is therefore not expected to delimit recently diverged species; the unresolved polytomy should be interpreted as a lack of informative variation rather than as evidence against the distinctiveness of F. mardinensis.

The delimitation of F. mardinensis therefore rests on a consistent combination of morphological characters (tepal shape and pigmentation with yellow apical stripes and ciliate tufts, linear nectaries, purple anthers and longitudinally striped capsules), supported by its geographically restricted occurrence in Mardin Province. The molecular data are compatible with the generic placement of the species but do not test its delimitation. Several limitations should nevertheless be noted. Only a partial consensus sequence (472 unambiguous sites) could be obtained for F. armena, which reduces the number of informative sites and probably contributes to its unresolved placement. The two GenBank records available for F. zagrica are cloned sequences containing rearranged segments, and only a collinear region of KM435235 (positions 262–640) was used; the grouping of F. zagrica with F. ferganensis (BS = 95) should thus be treated with caution and not interpreted as evidence of phylogenetic relationships. In addition, ITS is a multi-copy region, and intragenomic variation among copies may blur the signal obtained from direct sequencing. Further sampling, improved sequences for F. armena and F. zagrica, and additional nuclear and plastid markers (e.g., matK, rbcL) will help to test the relationships of F. mardinensis more rigorously.

The geographical distribution of F. mardinensis is also relevant to its taxonomic and conservation assessment. The species is currently known from a restricted area in Mardin Province, where it occurs on stony north-facing slopes at approximately 1145 m above sea level. The reported distribution differs geographically from those indicated for the related taxa in the comparative distribution map. Nevertheless, geographical separation alone does not demonstrate independent evolutionary history; its significance should be evaluated alongside morphological and, where available, molecular evidence.

The discovery of F. mardinensis also emphasizes the importance of continued botanical exploration in southeastern Anatolia. Despite the considerable diversity of Fritillaria in Türkiye, localized populations and morphologically distinctive taxa may remain insufficiently documented. The recognition of the new species is therefore relevant not only to the taxonomy of the genus but also to regional biodiversity assessment and conservation planning.

Although the morphological evidence supports the recognition of F. mardinensis, additional investigations would be valuable for testing its evolutionary relationships with F. armena and F. zagrica. Additional molecular markers, expanded sampling across the geographical ranges of the three species, and quantitative assessments of morphological variation would help clarify their relationships and determine whether the diagnostic characters of F. mardinensis remain consistent across populations. Such work would provide an independent assessment of the species boundaries suggested by the present morphological study.

From a conservation perspective, the restricted distribution of F. mardinensis warrants particular attention. Fewer than 100 mature individuals were observed at the type locality, and grazing pressure was observed to affect the population. These observations, together with the limited known area of occupancy, indicate potential vulnerability to habitat degradation and population decline. Continued field monitoring, assessment of grazing impacts, and protection of the known habitat are therefore important priorities.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: Fritillaria mardinensis is distinguished from the morphologically related species F. armena and F. zagrica by a combination of vegetative, floral, and fruit characters. The most informative diagnostic features include its relatively elongated stem, distinctive tepal shapes and pigmentation, yellowish ciliate tufts at the tepal apices, narrow linear nectaries, purple anthers, and longitudinally dark-striped capsule. ITS phylogenetic inference places F. mardinensis within the main Fritillaria clade but does not resolve its relationship to closely related taxa. Although F. mardinensis differs by 6 bp from F. armena and by 23 bp from F. zagrica, its ITS distance to F. armena is larger than that to F. alburyana; ITS is therefore uninformative at the species level, and the delimitation of F. mardinensis rests on morphology. The combination of morphological and geographical evidence supports the description of F. mardinensis as a new species.
